The automat was a very practical, convenient, concept that worked very well for a long time--and it never entirely disappeared. Its decline was actually precipitated by changes in economy rather than any problem with the concept itself. You see, after WWII food prices rose consistently to where it required handling more and more coins to pay for your food at the Automat. Eventually, that became physically unwieldy. The government lagged on the introduction of larger denomination coins and we didn't have a vending machine technology that could reliably read paper bills until the '70s. Token systems might have solved the problem, but this eliminated the convenience of being able to quickly buy a meal out of pocket. You had to line-up at a change-maker counter when both entering and leaving. And so the great convenience of the Automat was lost. The changing physical nature of money made it unwieldy.

To address the handling of paper money fast food restaurants had to re-introduce human workers in a front-end role that had previously been made obsolete. But instead of returning to the sit-down restaurant or diner-style model again, they adopted a cued counter-service model which also better suited the use of drive-through service. This, however, demanded an extremely fast pace of serial production (the Automat could more efficiently cook in batches) and so highly standardized menus were imposed and an assembly-line approach was applied in the kitchen. Fast food became obsessed with Taylorization--the scientific management of labor and the obsessive study of labor ergonomics that precipitated the dehumanizing nature of fast food jobs.

But now the physical nature of money is changing again. We've replaced paper money and coin with debit cards and digital payment mechanisms using cell phones. Credit and debit cards have been around for a long time, but only relatively recently did their use become ubiquitous in the prime demographic segment of fast food, thus offering you an option to go cashless and not inconvenience too many people. And that was a choice of the banks. So now we have a form of money that makes the Automat model and the use of push-button ordering practical again. Thus we get things like Eatsa appearing and more elaborate and interesting things like the roller-coaster restaurant. Over time we'll see more elaborate automation employed for novelty-sake while simple automation--Automat walls, smart-lock lockers, order-by-phone counter service, touch screens with debit card readers--take up the mainstream. The human front-end jobs in fast food were always precarious because they had been obsolesced before. It was only a matter of time before we reinvented money again. It was never really about any sophisticated form of automation.

I don't think anyone would care about this change had it not been for blowhards like the Carl's Jr. CEO deliberately trying to make it a political issue. This was a change already in progress across the world. And it's not effecting the back-end so much. Automation in the kitchen remains a challenge. Fast food chains have always applied as much automation as they could there because of the obsession with Talyorization, but it never proved easy. The materials remain difficult for machines to physically handle without resulting in forms so standardized it makes the resulting food appear artificial. This is why fast food vending machines have made slow progress. We can process many foods that way, but the hard part is keeping the end result from looking like the product of a machine.

In Japan, where they long had a wider range of coinage values and a greater obsession with automation, they've long had fast food restaurants that consist of nothing but vending machines, with no human service at all. These go back into the late '70s and there's even a certain nostalgia today for these old machines. The food isn't that great--in appearance especially--but it was good enough for the truck driver or student wanting a quick meal. But these places are not designed for the kind of throughput of an American fast food restaurant. Any given machine is intended to store and serve up to several dozen of a food item per day whereas the usual fast food restaurant would dish out many hundreds to thousands. So these places were typically very small and in more out-of-the-way locations.
